newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong newspaper headlines-June 1.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong newspaper headlines-June 1.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- MING PAO -- About 2,000 People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops will enter Hong Kong minutes after the handover to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30. The rest of the Hong Kong garrison, which will total up to 6,000 soldiers, will arrive at dawn. Sources said Beijing took the image of the garrison very seriously and had instructed officials in charge of the media to make reporting of the PLA's entrance a priority.

-- SING TAO -- More than 40 Chinese overseas dissidents signed a letter urging the Chinese government to allow disgraced former Communist Party chief Zhao Ziyang to attend the Hong Kong handover ceremony.

-- TA KUNG PAO -- A big handover celebration party will be held at Workers' Stadium in Beijing on July 1, at which 18,000 artists from China and Hong Kong will perform. The party will wrap up with Hong Kong and mainland performers singing a tune called "Reunifications".
-- WEN WEI PO -- More than 100,000 application forms for Hong Kong's post-handover passport were handed out on Tuesday, with some people queuing since the early morning.

-- ECONOMIC TIMES -- Japan's Entertainment Television was in talks with Wharf over introducing its programmes to Hong Kong, with its 24-hour JET TV expected to be broadcast in the territory by September.
-- Rumours are rife in Beijing that Chinese authorities will close down the Shenzhen and Shanghai bourses for 10 days to prevent the stock market from being pushed too high by handover euphoria.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- The chairman and a director of H-share Guangshen Railway transferred 300 million yuan of the company's listing proceeds to a stock brokerage without the approval of the board, an investigation by mainland regulators revealed.
-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- Analysts said Cable & Wireless' chances of pushing into the mainland market were still cloudy despite its sale of 5.5 percent of Hongkong Telecom to state-owned China Telecom.
